newsitem.title: USA: Astronomers record first supernova collision.
newsitem.headline: Astronomers record first supernova collision.

text.p: Astronomers using the Hubble space telescope are witnessing for the first time a collision of two exploding stars, which is creating a spectacular display in a distant, turbulent galaxy.

The collision taking place 17 million light years from Earth is likely to last about 1,200 years, Johns Hopkins University astrophysicist William Blair said in a report to be presented on Tuesday at a meeting of the American Astronomical Society in Winston-Salem, North Carolina.

In the report Blair says the two stars probably were born and died together and exploded within 20,000 years of each other. When a massive star explodes, creating a supernova, it shoots out gas and debris in all directions at a speed of 22 million miles per hour (36 million km per hour), Johns Hopkins said in a release.
The shock wave from the explosion compresses the gas into a dense shell. When the shells of both exploding supernovas collided, the result was a brilliant light show.

"We have identified a case where we believe that there can be little doubt that the interacting shells from separate supernova explosions have been caught in the act," Blair said in his report. "This shock wave collision is the primary cause of the extreme luminosity seen for this object."
The collision is taking place in a galaxy known as NGC 6946, which Blair called a "veritable supernova factory" that has produced at least six supernovas since 1917.

He said if new supernova continue to be born in that part of the universe it could create a "superbubble" in which a large, expanding shell is powered by multiple supernovas and stellar winds from massive stars. But it will take several hundred thousand years to learn whether what was being witnessed today is the birth pangs of a supernova, he said.
